note: Starter rules. The path patterns are guesses at a common layout: change them to where things live in your repository before you trust any answer. Reference: docs/gates.md.

items.title: A check that can be run
items.note: No satisfied_by: the author fixes the brief and runs the gate again, or waives it in one line.

ask.question: Does this brief lack an acceptance check that someone could run and that comes back pass or fail?
ask.true: No acceptance check in the brief can be run as written, or none is named.
ask.false: The brief names at least one command, test or step with a pass or fail result.

ask.question: Does this brief say the change alters the shape of data that is already stored, changes a contract other code or another service reads, or introduces a pattern the codebase does not use yet?
ask.true: The brief describes a change to stored data shape, to an existing contract, or a new structural pattern.
ask.false: The brief describes a change inside existing structures and contracts.

ask.question: Does this brief say the change touches sign-in or access rules, payment, stored personal data, or deletes or rewrites data that already exists?
ask.true: The brief describes a change to access, payment, personal data, or a destructive change to existing data.
ask.false: The brief describes none of these.

items.title: Unit test
items.note: Path rule only: any source change owes a test file change, and a rename-only change is waived in one line. Add an 'ask' here if that proves too coarse.

items.title: Database or integration test
items.note: A run counts: where an existing suite already covers the change, such as a start-up test for a change in wiring, the author names it in a 'Ran integration-test: ...' line and the reviewer judges that. Take run_counts out if new behaviour here should always bring a new test.

ask.question: Could this change alter behaviour that only shows up against a real database or a started application: queries or writes, stored shapes, how components are wired together, scheduled jobs, or how HTTP requests are bound and answered?
ask.true: The change touches code that talks to the database or runs inside the started application, so a unit test with mocks could miss a break.
ask.false: The change is confined to pure logic, mapping, formatting, comments or renames that unit tests exercise without a database or a started application.

ask.question: Does this diff add or remove an endpoint, or change the name, type, nullability or meaning of a field, parameter or status code that an existing endpoint already exposes?
ask.true: The shape of what callers send or receive changes.
ask.false: Only the inside of a handler changes; callers send and receive the same shape.

items.title: User journey test
items.note: A new page owes at least a 'the page opens' line. A journey test is owed when the user does something across steps.

ask.question: Does this diff add or change a sequence of two or more actions that a user performs in the browser to reach a result, such as signing up, importing data, following an item or paying?
ask.true: A multi-step user flow is added, or a step of an existing flow changes what the user must do.
ask.false: The change is presentational, or changes one screen without changing the steps of a flow.

items.title: Run of a changed script
items.note: A script that runs against production rarely has a test, and a syntax check does not catch a wrong flag. So the evidence is a run of the commands the change adds or alters: 'Ran script-run: <command, where, what it printed>'. A read-only command can be run before the merge. Waive it for a change to comments only.

items.title: Security review
items.note: The scans (secrets, static analysis, dependencies) run on every change and are not decided here. This item decides the extra review.

ask.question: Does this diff change who can read or change which user's data, how a caller is identified, what a visitor who is not signed in can reach, what the system fetches from or sends to an outside address, or how a file or text supplied by a user is parsed or stored?
ask.true: The change affects access to data, the identity of the caller, the anonymous surface, outbound requests, or the handling of user-supplied files or text.
ask.false: The change affects none of these.

items.title: Architect review of a stored-data change
items.note: Migration files are one way to change stored data. Code that merges, repairs or backfills records when it runs is another: add the folders where yours lives to the paths.

ask.question: Does this change alter or delete data that is already stored, rather than only add new optional data?
ask.true: Existing rows, nodes, columns or properties are rewritten, removed or given a new meaning.
ask.false: The change only adds new optional structures or data.

items.title: Live model run
items.note: A live run costs money, so the gate only says it is owed. A person decides whether to run it.

items.title: Approval of a change to the gate, its rules or its lessons
items.note: These files decide how much checking every later change gets, so a change to them is a person's to approve. In CI the gate and the rules are read from the base branch (see ci/handover-gate.yml), so a pull request cannot loosen the rules that judge it.
